content:
# Phase 7 interview questions

**Q. Why is Redis fast?**
A. It works in memory, runs a single-threaded event loop without locking, uses efficient data structures, and has a simple protocol.

**Q. Redis data types?**
A. String, Hash, List, Set, Sorted Set, plus Streams, Bitmaps, HyperLogLog and Geo.

**Q. Explain cache-aside.**
A. Read from the cache. On a miss, load from the DB and populate the cache with a TTL. On writes, update the DB and evict the cache entry.

**Q. How do you keep the cache consistent with the DB?**
A. Evict on write (rather than update), use TTLs as a safety net, keep the DB as the source of truth, and don't cache data that needs strict real-time accuracy.

**Q. What is a cache stampede and how do you prevent it?**
A. Many requests reload the same expired hot key at once. Prevent it with a single-flight lock (`@Cacheable(sync=true)`), early refresh and jittered TTLs.

**Q. How do you share sessions across multiple instances?**
A. Spring Session with Redis, or go stateless with JWT.

**Q. How do you implement a distributed lock with Redis?**
A. `SET key owner NX PX ttl`, release with an atomic owner check (Lua), or use Redisson/ShedLock.

**Q. RDB vs AOF?**
A. RDB takes periodic snapshots (compact, possible data loss). AOF logs every write (durable, larger). They can be combined.

**Q. What eviction policy for a cache?**
A. allkeys-lru (or allkeys-lfu).

**Q. Redis vs Memcached?**
A. Redis has rich data types, persistence, replication, pub/sub and Lua. Memcached is a simple multi-threaded string cache.

name: JavaScript Core Concepts
description: let/const, types, ==/===, closures, this, destructuring, spread, array methods
content:
# JavaScript core concepts

## var vs let vs const
```js
var a = 1;      // function-scoped, hoisted, can be redeclared: avoid
let b = 2;      // block-scoped, can be reassigned
const c = 3;    // block-scoped, can't be reassigned
const arr = [1]; arr.push(2);   // OK: const freezes the BINDING, not the object
```
- Use `const` by default, and `let` when the value must change. Never `var`.

## == vs ===
```js
0 == "0"        // true  (type coercion)
0 === "0"       // false (different types)
null == undefined   // true
null === undefined  // false
```
- **Always use `===`.** `==` converts types in surprising ways.

**Falsy values:** `false, 0, "", null, undefined, NaN`. Everything else is truthy (even `"0"` and `[]`).

## Closures
A function **remembers the variables of the place where it was created**, even after that outer function has finished.

```js
function makeCounter() {
  let count = 0;                 // private variable
  return function () {
    count++;                     // still accessible later
    return count;
  };
}
const next = makeCounter();
next(); // 1
next(); // 2
```
**Line by line**
- `makeCounter` returns an inner function. Normally `count` would disappear when `makeCounter` ends.
- The inner function **closes over** `count`, keeping it alive. Nobody else can touch `count`, so we get privacy.
- **Analogy:** a backpack. The function carries its birthplace's variables in a backpack wherever it goes.
- React hooks rely on closures. **Stale closures** (a callback seeing an old state value) are a common bug.

## this
- In a normal function, `this` depends on **how the function is called** (`obj.method()` → obj).
- **Arrow functions have no own `this`**: they use the `this` of the surrounding code. That's why arrows are handy in callbacks.

## Modern syntax you must read fluently
```js
const member = { name: "Rahim", phone: "017...", po: { code: "PO-07" } };

const { name, po: { code } } = member;        // destructuring
const [first, ...rest] = [10, 20, 30];        // first=10, rest=[20,30]
const copy = { ...member, name: "Karim" };    // spread: shallow copy + override
const merged = [...[1, 2], ...[3]];           // [1,2,3]
const city = member.address?.city ?? "N/A";   // optional chaining + nullish coalescing
const greet = (n = "Guest") => `Hello ${n}`;  // default param + template literal
```
- Destructuring pulls fields out into variables.
- Spread `...` copies or merges. It's essential for **immutable state updates** in React.
- `?.` stops and returns `undefined` instead of throwing when something is null.
- `??` uses the right side only when the left is `null`/`undefined` (unlike `||`, which also replaces `0` and `""`).

## Array methods (used constantly in React)
```js
const loans = [ { id: 1, amt: 5000, active: true }, { id: 2, amt: 8000, active: false } ];

loans.map(l => l.amt);                          // [5000, 8000]   transform each
loans.filter(l => l.active);                    // [{id:1...}]    keep some
loans.reduce((sum, l) => sum + l.amt, 0);       // 13000          combine into one
loans.find(l => l.id === 2);                    // {id:2...}      first match
loans.some(l => !l.active);                     // true           any match?
loans.every(l => l.amt > 1000);                 // true           all match?
[...loans].sort((a, b) => b.amt - a.amt);       // sort a COPY (sort mutates!)
```
- `map`, `filter` and `reduce` return **new** arrays/values and don't mutate the original. React state must not be mutated.
- `sort` **mutates** in place, so copy first with `[...arr]` (or use `toSorted()` in modern JS).

description: Rendering, code splitting, error boundaries, security, build
content:
# React advanced and performance ## How rendering works 1. State or props change → React **re-runs** the component function (render). 2. It builds a new **virtual DOM** tree and **diffs** it with the previous one (reconciliation). 3. Only the **real DOM changes** that are actually needed are applied (commit). **Analogy:** a spot-the-difference puzzle. React compares the old and new pictures and repaints only the differences instead of the whole wall. A re-render happens when: the component's state changes, its parent re-renders, or a context it uses changes. ## Code splitting with lazy loading ```tsx const Reports = lazy(() => import("./pages/Reports")); // separate JS chunk }> ``` - The Reports code downloads **only when the user opens it**, so the first page loads faster. - `Suspense fallback`: what to show while the chunk loads. ## Error boundaries ```tsx import { ErrorBoundary } from "react-error-boundary"; Something went wrong in this panel.

}> ``` - If `PortfolioChart` throws during render, only that panel shows the fallback, and the whole app doesn't go blank. (Error boundaries catch **render** errors, not async errors in event handlers.) ## Performance checklist - Keep state **as close as possible** to where it is used. - Virtualize long lists (`@tanstack/react-virtual`): render only the visible rows. - `React.memo` / `useMemo` / `useCallback` only for measured problems. - Debounce search inputs. - Use the React DevTools **Profiler** to see what re-renders and why. ## Frontend security - React escapes `{text}` automatically. **Avoid `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`** (sanitize with DOMPurify if you must use it). - Never store secrets in frontend code: everything in the bundle is public. - Prefer HttpOnly cookies / in-memory tokens over localStorage for tokens. - The backend must always re-check permissions. ## Build and deploy (Vite) ```bash npm create vite@latest loan-web -- --template react-ts npm run dev # dev server with hot reload npm run build # optimized static files in dist/ ``` - `dist/` is just static HTML/JS/CSS. Serve it with Nginx (in Docker) and proxy `/api` to the backend. Configure Nginx to fall back to `index.html` for client-side routes (`try_files $uri /index.html;`).

content:
# Phase 8 interview questions

**Q. let vs const vs var?**
A. var is function-scoped and hoisted. let and const are block-scoped. const can't be reassigned (but objects stay mutable).

**Q. == vs ===?**
A. `==` converts types before comparing. `===` compares type and value. Always use `===`.

**Q. What is a closure?**
A. A function that remembers the variables of the scope where it was created, even after that scope has finished.

**Q. Explain the event loop output of: log 1, setTimeout 2, promise 3, log 4.**
A. 1, 4, 3, 2. Sync code first, then microtasks (promises), then macrotasks (timers).

**Q. Props vs state?**
A. Props are inputs passed from the parent and are read-only. State is the component's own data, and changing it with the setter triggers a re-render.

**Q. Why do lists need keys?**
A. So that React can match items between renders and update, reorder or remove the right DOM nodes efficiently. Use stable unique IDs, not indexes.

**Q. What does the useEffect dependency array do?**
A. It controls when the effect re-runs: `[]` once after mount, `[x]` when x changes, none after every render. The cleanup runs before the next run and on unmount.

**Q. useMemo vs useCallback?**
A. useMemo caches a computed value. useCallback caches a function reference. Both recompute when their dependencies change.

**Q. What is prop drilling and how do you avoid it?**
A. Passing props through many layers that don't need them. Avoid it with Context, composition or a state library.

**Q. Controlled vs uncontrolled inputs?**
A. Controlled: the value comes from React state with onChange. Uncontrolled: the DOM holds the value and you read it through a ref (React Hook Form uses this for performance).

**Q. Why use TanStack Query instead of useEffect + fetch?**
A. It provides caching, deduplication, background refetching, retries, loading/error states and invalidation after mutations, with far less hand-written code.

**Q. How do you protect routes in React?**
A. A guard component that checks the auth state and redirects with `<Navigate>`. The backend must still enforce authorization, because frontend checks are only UX.

**Q. What is the virtual DOM?**
A. An in-memory tree of UI elements. React diffs the new tree with the old one and applies only the needed changes to the real DOM.

**Q. interface vs type in TypeScript?**
A. Both describe shapes. Interfaces can be extended or merged. Types can also express unions, intersections and mapped types.

content:
# Code quality

## Clean code habits (say these in a viva)
- **Meaningful names:** `calculateOverdueAmount()`, not `calc2()`.
- **Small functions** that do one thing.
- **No magic numbers:** `MAX_LOAN_AMOUNT`, not `500000` scattered around.
- **DRY** (Don't Repeat Yourself), but don't over-abstract too early.
- **Fail fast:** validate inputs at the boundary.
- **Comments explain why**, not what.

```java
// ✗ Before
public double c(List<Loan> l) {
    double t = 0;
    for (Loan x : l) if (x.s == 2 && x.d.isBefore(LocalDate.now())) t += x.a * 0.02;
    return t;
}

// ✓ After
private static final BigDecimal LATE_FEE_RATE = new BigDecimal("0.02");

public BigDecimal totalLateFees(List<Loan> loans) {
    return loans.stream()
            .filter(Loan::isOverdue)
            .map(loan -> loan.getOutstanding().multiply(LATE_FEE_RATE))
            .reduce(BigDecimal.ZERO, BigDecimal::add);
}
```
**Why the second is better**
- The name says what it does. `isOverdue()` hides the status/date details inside the Loan class (encapsulation).
- The magic number `0.02` becomes a named constant.
- `BigDecimal` instead of `double` for money.
- No cryptic one-letter variables.

## Tools

| Tool | Checks |
|---|---|
| **JaCoCo** | Test coverage % (lines/branches) |
| **SonarQube / SonarCloud** | Bugs, code smells, duplication, security hotspots, a quality gate |
| **Checkstyle / Spotless** | Code formatting and style |
| **SpotBugs / PMD** | Common bug patterns |
| **ESLint + Prettier** | JS/TS linting and formatting |
| **OWASP Dependency-Check / Dependabot** | Vulnerable libraries |

```xml
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.jacoco</groupId>
  <artifactId>jacoco-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>0.8.12</version>
  <executions>
    <execution><goals><goal>prepare-agent</goal></goals></execution>
    <execution><id>report</id><phase>verify</phase><goals><goal>report</goal></goals></execution>
  </executions>
</plugin>
```
- `prepare-agent`: attaches the coverage agent while the tests run. `report` writes an HTML report to `target/site/jacoco`.
- **Coverage is a guide, not a goal.** 80% coverage with weak assertions is worse than 60% with meaningful tests. Focus on business rules (interest, overdue, balance).

## Code review checklist
Correctness and edge cases → tests included → security (input validation, authorization) → performance (N+1, missing indexes) → readability → no secrets committed.

name: Phase 9 — Interview Questions
description: Quick Q&A revision for testing
content:
# Phase 9 interview questions

**Q. Unit vs integration test?**
A. A unit test checks one class in isolation with dependencies mocked (fast). An integration test checks several parts working together with real infrastructure such as the DB or HTTP (slower).

**Q. What is the test pyramid?**
A. Many unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few E2E tests, because higher-level tests are slower and more brittle.

**Q. Mock vs stub vs spy?**
A. A stub returns canned data. A mock also verifies interactions. A spy wraps a real object and lets you override parts of it.

**Q. @Mock vs @MockitoBean (@MockBean)?**
A. @Mock is a plain Mockito mock for unit tests without Spring. @MockitoBean replaces a bean inside the Spring test context.

**Q. @WebMvcTest vs @SpringBootTest?**
A. @WebMvcTest loads only the web layer (fast, services mocked). @SpringBootTest loads the full application context.

**Q. Why Testcontainers instead of H2?**
A. It tests against the same database engine as production (SQL dialect, types, constraints, migrations), so the tests are trustworthy.

**Q. How do you test a method that throws?**
A. `assertThrows(Expected.class, () -> call())`, then assert on the message or state, and verify that no side effects happened.

**Q. What is TDD?**
A. Test-Driven Development: write a failing test (red), write the minimum code to pass (green), then refactor. Repeat.

**Q. What does good code coverage mean?**
A. Coverage shows which code ran during tests, not whether behaviour was verified. Aim for meaningful tests of critical logic rather than a number.

**Q. How do you test a React component?**
A. Render it with React Testing Library, interact as a user (type, click), assert on visible output, and mock the API with MSW.

name: Git
description: Daily commands, branching, merge vs rebase, conflicts, workflows
content:
# Git

Git is a **version control system**: it records snapshots of your project so you can go back, compare, and work in parallel on branches.
**Analogy:** save points in a video game, plus parallel universes (branches) that you can later merge back together.

## Daily workflow
```bash
git clone https://github.com/you/loan-system.git
git checkout -b feature/repayment-api        # create and switch to a new branch
# ... edit files ...
git status                                    # what changed?
git add src/main/java/.../RepaymentService.java
git commit -m "feat(repayment): record repayment and update outstanding"
git pull --rebase origin main                 # get the latest main, replay my commits on top
git push -u origin feature/repayment-api      # publish the branch
# open a Pull Request -> review -> merge
```
**Line by line**
- `checkout -b`: a new branch, so `main` stays stable while you work.
- `git add`: moves changes to the **staging area** (choose what goes into the next commit).
- `git commit -m`: saves a snapshot with a message. Use clear messages, e.g. the **Conventional Commits** style: `feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, `refactor:`, `test:`.
- `pull --rebase`: avoids extra merge commits and keeps history linear.
- `push -u`: uploads and sets the upstream, so later a plain `git push` works.

**The three areas:** working directory (your files) → staging area (`git add`) → repository (`git commit`).

## Merge vs rebase
```
main:     A---B---C
feature:       \---D---E

merge:    A---B---C---M        (M = merge commit, history kept as it happened)
               \---D---E/

rebase:   A---B---C---D'---E'  (feature commits replayed on top: a linear history)
```
- **Merge:** safe, keeps the true history, but adds merge commits.
- **Rebase:** a cleaner, linear history, but it **rewrites commits**. **Never rebase commits that others have already pulled** (shared branches).
- **Analogy:** merge is stapling two notebooks together. Rebase is rewriting your notes neatly onto the end of the main notebook.

## Resolving a conflict
```
<<<<<<< HEAD
BigDecimal rate = new BigDecimal("0.12");
=======
BigDecimal rate = new BigDecimal("0.10");
>>>>>>> feature/new-rate
```
- Both branches changed the same line. Edit the file to the correct final version, delete the markers, then `git add` and `git commit` (or `git rebase --continue`).

## Undoing things
```bash
git restore file.txt              # discard unstaged changes to a file
git restore --staged file.txt     # unstage
git commit --amend                # fix the last commit (only if not pushed)
git revert <sha>                  # NEW commit that undoes an old one (safe on shared branches)
git reset --soft HEAD~1           # undo the last commit, keep the changes staged
git stash / git stash pop         # put work aside temporarily
git log --oneline --graph         # view history
git cherry-pick <sha>             # copy one commit onto the current branch
```
- `revert` vs `reset`: **revert is safe for shared history** (it adds a commit). `reset --hard` destroys work and rewrites history.

## Branching strategies
- **GitHub Flow:** `main` is always deployable. Short-lived feature branches go through PRs. Simple, and good for CI/CD.
- **Git Flow:** `main`, `develop`, `feature/*`, `release/*`, `hotfix/*`. For scheduled releases.
- **Trunk-based:** everyone merges small changes to main often, using feature flags.

`.gitignore`: never commit `target/`, `node_modules/`, `.env` or secrets.

name: Linux and Servers
description: Essential commands, processes, logs, permissions, Nginx reverse proxy
content:
# Linux and servers

Most servers run Linux. You should be comfortable on the command line.

```bash
# Files and navigation
pwd; ls -la; cd /var/log
cat app.log | less
tail -f /var/log/loan-api/app.log          # follow the log live
grep -i "error" app.log | tail -n 50       # last 50 error lines
grep -rn "OutOfMemory" /var/log/           # search recursively with line numbers
find / -name "*.jar" -size +50M 2>/dev/null

# Processes and ports
ps aux | grep java                         # is the app running?
top / htop                                 # CPU and memory usage
kill -15 <pid>                             # ask nicely to stop (SIGTERM)
kill -9 <pid>                              # force kill (last resort)
ss -tulpn | grep 8080                      # which process listens on 8080?

# Disk and memory
df -h                                      # disk space
du -sh /var/lib/postgresql                 # folder size
free -h                                    # memory

# Permissions
chmod 750 deploy.sh                        # owner rwx, group r-x, others none
chown app:app /opt/loan-api -R

# Networking
curl -i http://localhost:8080/actuator/health
ping db.internal; nslookup api.pksf.org.bd

# Services (systemd)
sudo systemctl status loan-api
sudo systemctl restart loan-api
journalctl -u loan-api -f                  # service logs
```
**Key explanations**
- `tail -f`: watch new log lines as they are written, the first thing to do when debugging production.
- `|` (pipe): sends one command's output into the next (`grep` filters, `tail` keeps the last lines).
- `2>/dev/null`: hides error messages (stream 2 = stderr).
- `kill -15` lets Spring Boot shut down gracefully (finish requests, close DB connections). `-9` kills it instantly.
- `chmod 750`: each digit is owner / group / others, and r=4 + w=2 + x=1. So 7 = rwx, 5 = r-x, 0 = none.

## Nginx as a reverse proxy

```nginx
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name app.pksf.org.bd;
    ssl_certificate     /etc/ssl/certs/app.crt;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/ssl/private/app.key;

    root /usr/share/nginx/html;              # React build files
    location / {
        try_files $uri /index.html;          # SPA: unknown paths -> index.html
    }

    location /api/ {
        proxy_pass http://loan-api:8080;     # forward to Spring Boot
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }
}
```
**Line by line**
- A **reverse proxy** sits in front of your apps: it terminates HTTPS, serves static files, and forwards API calls. **Analogy:** a receptionist who greets every visitor and walks them to the right office.
- `ssl_certificate`: HTTPS is handled here, so the app itself can speak plain HTTP inside the private network.
- `try_files $uri /index.html`: lets React Router handle URLs like `/members/42` on refresh.
- `proxy_pass`: forwards `/api/...` to the backend.
- `X-Forwarded-*` headers: tell the app the real client IP and the original protocol (set `server.forward-headers-strategy=framework` in Spring).

content:
**Docker** packages an app **with everything it needs** (runtime, libraries, config) into an **image** that runs the same everywhere.
**Analogy:** a shipping container. Whatever is inside, every ship, crane and truck handles it the same way. "Works on my machine" becomes "works on every machine".

name: Docker Concepts and Commands
description: Image vs container, layers, volumes, networks, essential commands
content:
# Docker concepts and commands

| Concept | Meaning | Analogy |
|---|---|---|
| **Image** | A read-only template (app + runtime + OS libraries) | A recipe / a class |
| **Container** | A running instance of an image | A cooked dish / an object |
| **Layer** | Each Dockerfile instruction makes a cached layer | Stacked transparent sheets |
| **Registry** | Stores images (Docker Hub, GHCR, Harbor) | An app store |
| **Volume** | Persistent storage outside the container | An external hard drive |
| **Network** | Lets containers talk by name | A private office LAN |

**Container vs VM:** a VM includes a whole guest OS (heavy, minutes to boot). Containers **share the host's kernel** and only isolate processes (light, seconds to start).
**Analogy:** VMs are separate houses, each with its own plumbing. Containers are apartments in one building, sharing the plumbing but each with its own locked door.

```bash
docker build -t loan-api:1.0 .                 # build an image from the Dockerfile in the current folder
docker images                                  # list images
docker run -d --name loan-api -p 8080:8080 \
  -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod \
  -e DB_PASSWORD=secret \
  loan-api:1.0                                 # run in the background
docker ps                                      # running containers (-a for all)
docker logs -f loan-api                        # follow the logs
docker exec -it loan-api sh                    # open a shell inside the container
docker stop loan-api && docker rm loan-api     # stop and remove
docker run -d --name pg -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=pw -p 5432:5432 postgres:16   # DB with a named volume
docker tag loan-api:1.0 ghcr.io/you/loan-api:1.0
docker push ghcr.io/you/loan-api:1.0           # upload to a registry
docker system prune                            # clean up unused data
```
**Line by line**
- `-t loan-api:1.0`: name:tag. **Avoid `latest` in production**: use explicit versions so you know exactly what's running.
- `-d`: detached (background).
- `-p 8080:8080`: **host port : container port**. Without it, the app isn't reachable from outside.
- `-e`: environment variables. This is how config and secrets get in (Spring maps `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` → `spring.datasource.url`).
- `exec -it ... sh`: debug inside a running container.
- `-v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data`: the DB files live in a **volume**. Removing the container doesn't delete your data.
- A container should run **one main process** and be **disposable**: anything important lives in volumes or external services.

name: Writing a Dockerfile
description: Multi-stage build for Spring Boot and React, best practices
content:
# Writing a Dockerfile

## Spring Boot: multi-stage build

```dockerfile
# ---------- Stage 1: build ----------
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn -q dependency:go-offline              # cache dependencies in their own layer
COPY src ./src
RUN mvn -q package -DskipTests

# ---------- Stage 2: run ----------
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app
RUN addgroup -S app && adduser -S app -G app  # don't run as root
COPY --from=build /app/target/*.jar app.jar
USER app
EXPOSE 8080
ENV JAVA_OPTS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75"
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:8080/actuator/health || exit 1
ENTRYPOINT ["sh", "-c", "java $JAVA_OPTS -jar app.jar"]
```
**Line by line**
- **Multi-stage:** stage 1 has Maven and the JDK (big) to **build**. Stage 2 copies only the JAR into a small **JRE** image. The final image is ~200 MB instead of ~800 MB, and contains no build tools (more secure).
- `FROM ... AS build`: names the stage so that we can copy from it later.
- `WORKDIR /app`: like `cd`, and it creates the folder.
- `COPY pom.xml` **before** `COPY src`: Docker caches layers. If only the code changes, the slow "download dependencies" layer is reused. **Order instructions from least to most frequently changing.**
- `-DskipTests`: tests run in CI before the image is built.
- `adduser` + `USER app`: if the app is hacked, the attacker isn't root.
- `COPY --from=build`: takes the JAR from stage 1.
- `EXPOSE 8080`: documentation only. It doesn't publish the port (`-p` does).
- `MaxRAMPercentage=75`: the JVM sizes its heap from the **container's** memory limit.
- `HEALTHCHECK`: Docker marks the container unhealthy if `/actuator/health` fails.
- `ENTRYPOINT [...]`: the command that runs at start. `sh -c` lets `$JAVA_OPTS` expand.

## React: build, then serve with Nginx
```dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci                                     # exact versions from package-lock
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM nginx:1.27-alpine
COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
COPY --from=build /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html
EXPOSE 80
```
- `npm ci`: a clean, reproducible install (faster than `npm install` and respects the lockfile).
- The final image is just Nginx + static files, with no Node.js in production.

## .dockerignore
```
target/
node_modules/
.git/
.env
```
- Keeps the build context small and stops secrets from being copied into the image.

**Best practices summary:** small base images (alpine/distroless), multi-stage builds, a non-root user, pinned versions, no secrets in the image (pass them at runtime), one process per container, and scan images (Trivy).

name: Docker Compose
description: Running the full stack locally with one command
content:
# Docker Compose

**Compose** defines several containers (app, DB, Redis, Keycloak) in one YAML file and starts them together.
**Analogy:** a band's setlist. One command and all the musicians start playing together, in the right order.

```yaml
# docker-compose.yml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: loans
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}         # from the .env file
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U app -d loans"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 10

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine

  keycloak:
    image: quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.0
    command: start-dev --import-realm
    environment:
      KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USERNAME: admin
      KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD: ${KC_ADMIN_PASSWORD}
    volumes:
      - ./keycloak/realm-pksf.json:/opt/keycloak/data/import/realm-pksf.json
    ports:
      - "8180:8080"

  api:
    build: ./backend
    environment:
      SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: docker
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/loans
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME: app
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}
      SPRING_DATA_REDIS_HOST: redis
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy              # wait until Postgres is really ready
      redis:
        condition: service_started
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"

  web:
    build: ./frontend
    ports:
      - "80:80"
    depends_on: [api]

volumes:
  pgdata:
```
```bash
docker compose up -d --build     # build and start everything
docker compose logs -f api       # follow one service's logs
docker compose down              # stop and remove the containers (volumes are kept)
docker compose down -v           # ... and delete the volumes (wipes the DB!)
```
**Line by line**
- `services:`: each key is a container. **The service name is also its hostname** on the shared network, so the API connects to `db:5432`, not `localhost`.
- `${DB_PASSWORD}`: read from a `.env` file next to the compose file (which stays out of Git).
- `volumes: pgdata:/var/lib/...`: the data survives `down`/`up`.
- `healthcheck` + `depends_on: condition: service_healthy`: the API starts only after Postgres accepts connections. Plain `depends_on` only waits for the container to *start*, not to be *ready*.
- `--import-realm`: Keycloak loads a pre-configured realm, so reviewers get a working login instantly.
- `build: ./backend`: build the image from that folder's Dockerfile.

**For the portfolio:** a reviewer should be able to run `git clone` + `docker compose up` and have the whole system working. That impresses interviewers.

name: Kubernetes
description: Pods, deployments, services, config, probes, scaling, ingress
content:
**Kubernetes (K8s)** runs and manages containers across many machines: it restarts crashed ones, scales them, rolls out updates and balances traffic.
**Analogy:** if Docker containers are shipping containers, Kubernetes is the **port authority**. It decides which ship (node) carries what, replaces lost containers, and keeps the schedule running.

name: Kubernetes Core Concepts
description: Cluster, node, pod, deployment, service, namespace, kubectl
content:
# Kubernetes core concepts

| Object | What it is | Analogy |
|---|---|---|
| **Cluster** | The control plane + worker nodes | The whole port |
| **Node** | A machine (VM/server) that runs pods | A ship |
| **Pod** | The smallest unit: 1+ containers sharing a network/IP | A container box on the ship |
| **Deployment** | Keeps N identical pods running, handles rolling updates | The manager who keeps "3 cooks on duty" |
| **ReplicaSet** | Created by the Deployment, maintains the pod count | The roster |
| **Service** | A stable IP/DNS name + load balancing over pods | The restaurant's phone number (whichever cook is free answers) |
| **Ingress** | HTTP routing from outside (host/path → service) | The main gate with signposts |
| **ConfigMap / Secret** | Configuration / sensitive configuration | Notice board / locked drawer |
| **Namespace** | A virtual partition (dev, test, prod) | Separate floors in a building |
| **PersistentVolumeClaim** | A request for durable storage | Renting a storage locker |
| **StatefulSet** | Like a Deployment, but with stable identity and storage (databases) | Named reserved seats |

**The control plane:** API server (all commands go through it), etcd (the cluster's database), scheduler (picks a node for each pod), controller manager (keeps reality matching the desired state).

**Declarative model:** you describe the **desired state** ("3 replicas of loan-api:1.4") in YAML, and K8s keeps working until reality matches. Kill a pod and a new one appears.

```bash
kubectl get pods -n loans                     # list pods in a namespace
kubectl get deploy,svc,ingress -n loans
kubectl describe pod loan-api-7c9f-abc -n loans   # events: why is it failing?
kubectl logs -f loan-api-7c9f-abc -n loans    # app logs
kubectl logs --previous <pod>                 # logs of the crashed previous container
kubectl exec -it <pod> -n loans -- sh         # shell inside the pod
kubectl apply -f k8s/                         # create/update from YAML files
kubectl rollout status deploy/loan-api -n loans
kubectl rollout undo deploy/loan-api -n loans # roll back to the previous version
kubectl scale deploy/loan-api --replicas=5 -n loans
kubectl port-forward svc/loan-api 8080:80 -n loans   # reach a service from your laptop
```
**Debugging common pod states**
- `CrashLoopBackOff`: the app starts and crashes repeatedly. Check `logs --previous` (often a bad config or the DB being unreachable).
- `ImagePullBackOff`: wrong image name/tag or missing registry credentials.
- `Pending`: no node has enough CPU/memory, or the PVC can't be bound. Check `describe`.
- `OOMKilled`: the container exceeded its memory limit. Raise the limit or fix the heap settings.

name: Kubernetes Manifests
description: Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Secret, probes, resources, HPA, Ingress YAML
content:
# Kubernetes manifests explained

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: loan-api-config
  namespace: loans
data:
  SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: "prod"
  SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: "jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/loans"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: loan-api-secret
  namespace: loans
type: Opaque
stringData:
  SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD: "change-me"
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: loan-api
  namespace: loans
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: loan-api }
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate: { maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1 }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: loan-api }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: loan-api
          image: ghcr.io/you/loan-api:1.4.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef: { name: loan-api-config }
            - secretRef: { name: loan-api-secret }
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "250m", memory: "512Mi" }
            limits:   { cpu: "1",    memory: "1Gi" }
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080 }
            initialDelaySeconds: 20
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 }
            initialDelaySeconds: 40
            periodSeconds: 20
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: loan-api
  namespace: loans
spec:
  selector: { app: loan-api }
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
  type: ClusterIP
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: loan-ingress
  namespace: loans
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
    - hosts: [api.pksf.org.bd]
      secretName: api-tls
  rules:
    - host: api.pksf.org.bd
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service: { name: loan-api, port: { number: 80 } }
---
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: loan-api
  namespace: loans
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: loan-api }
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 70 }
```

**Line by line**
- `---`: separates several objects in one file.
- **ConfigMap:** non-secret settings as key-value pairs.
- **Secret:** sensitive values. `stringData` lets you write plain text, which K8s stores **base64-encoded, not encrypted** by default. In real setups, enable encryption at rest or use Sealed Secrets / External Secrets / Vault, and never commit real secrets.
- `replicas: 3`: always keep 3 pods running.
- `selector.matchLabels` must match `template.metadata.labels`: that's how the Deployment knows which pods are "its own".
- `RollingUpdate maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1`: during an update, start one new pod, wait until it is ready, then remove one old pod. **Zero downtime.**
- `envFrom`: injects all ConfigMap/Secret keys as environment variables, which Spring Boot reads automatically.
- `resources.requests`: what the scheduler **reserves** (250m = a quarter of a CPU core). `limits`: the hard ceiling. Going over the memory limit gets the container OOMKilled, and over the CPU limit gets it throttled.
- **readinessProbe:** "Can I receive traffic?" Until it passes, the Service doesn't send requests to this pod (e.g. while it warms up or loses its DB).
- **livenessProbe:** "Am I still alive?" If it fails repeatedly, K8s **restarts** the container (it is stuck). Don't make liveness depend on the DB, or a DB outage will restart every pod.
- **Analogy:** readiness = "the shop sign says OPEN". Liveness = "the shopkeeper is still breathing".
- **Service `ClusterIP`:** an internal, stable address `loan-api.loans.svc.cluster.local`, load balanced across all ready pods with the label `app: loan-api`. Other types: `NodePort` (a port on every node) and `LoadBalancer` (a cloud load balancer).
- `port: 80` → `targetPort: 8080`: callers use port 80, and the traffic goes to the container's 8080.
- **Ingress:** routes external HTTPS for `api.pksf.org.bd` to the service. It needs an ingress controller (e.g. ingress-nginx). `tls.secretName` holds the certificate (often managed by cert-manager).
- **HPA:** if the average CPU goes above 70% of the *requests*, add pods (up to 10). When it drops, scale down (never below 3). It needs metrics-server.

**Helm** packages these YAMLs as templated **charts**, with per-environment values (`values-prod.yaml`).

name: CI/CD with GitHub Actions
description: Pipeline stages, build, test, image push, deploy
content:
# CI/CD with GitHub Actions

- **CI (Continuous Integration):** every push automatically builds and tests the code, so broken code is caught within minutes.
- **CD (Continuous Delivery/Deployment):** every passing build is automatically packaged and deployed (to staging, and to production after approval).

**Analogy:** a factory assembly line with quality checks. Each part is inspected automatically at every station, and only products that pass every check are shipped.

**Typical pipeline:** checkout → build → unit tests → integration tests → code quality/security scan → build the Docker image → push to the registry → deploy to staging → (approval) → deploy to production.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI/CD

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Java 21
        uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: "21"
          cache: maven

      - name: Build and test (unit + Testcontainers integration)
        run: mvn -B verify
        working-directory: backend

      - name: Frontend lint, test and build
        working-directory: frontend
        run: |
          npm ci
          npm run lint
          npm test -- --run
          npm run build

  docker:
    needs: build-test                          # runs only if the tests passed
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'        # only on main, not on PRs
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          context: ./backend
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}/loan-api:${{ github.sha }}

  deploy:
    needs: docker
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production                    # can require a manual approval in GitHub settings
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
        env:
          KUBECONFIG_DATA: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}
        run: |
          echo "$KUBECONFIG_DATA" > kubeconfig
          kubectl --kubeconfig kubeconfig -n loans set image deploy/loan-api \
            loan-api=ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}/loan-api:${{ github.sha }}
          kubectl --kubeconfig kubeconfig -n loans rollout status deploy/loan-api --timeout=180s
```

**Line by line**
- `on: push / pull_request`: when the pipeline runs. PRs get build + test only, and `main` also gets deployed.
- `jobs`: run in parallel by default. `needs:` creates an order (test → docker → deploy).
- `runs-on: ubuntu-latest`: a fresh virtual machine for each run (Docker is available, so **Testcontainers works**).
- `actions/checkout`: downloads your repository's code.
- `setup-java ... cache: maven`: installs the JDK and caches `~/.m2` for faster builds.
- `mvn -B verify`: batch mode. Compiles, runs unit tests (Surefire) and integration tests (Failsafe).
- `npm ci`, `lint`, `test`, `build`: the frontend quality gate.
- `if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'`: only publish images from main.
- `secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN`: an automatic token that can push to GitHub's container registry. **Secrets are never written in YAML.** Store them in the repo settings.
- Tag = `github.sha` (the commit hash): every image maps to an exact commit, so rollback is just redeploying an older tag.
- `environment: production`: GitHub can require a reviewer to approve before this job runs.
- `kubectl set image` + `rollout status`: triggers the rolling update and **fails the pipeline** if the new pods don't become ready, at which point you can `rollout undo`.

**GitOps alternative:** CI only updates the image tag in a Git repo of manifests, and **Argo CD / Flux** syncs the cluster to match Git.

**Deployment strategies:** rolling (the default), **blue-green** (two full environments, switch traffic at once, instant rollback), **canary** (send 5% of traffic to the new version first, then increase).

name: Phase 10 — Interview Questions
description: Quick Q&A revision for DevOps
content:
# Phase 10 interview questions

**Q. merge vs rebase?**
A. Merge combines histories with a merge commit and keeps the true history. Rebase replays commits on a new base, giving a linear history, but it rewrites commits, so never rebase shared branches.

**Q. git revert vs git reset?**
A. Revert creates a new commit that undoes an old one (safe for shared branches). Reset moves the branch pointer and can discard commits (rewrites history).

**Q. Image vs container?**
A. An image is a read-only template. A container is a running instance of an image.

**Q. Container vs virtual machine?**
A. Containers share the host kernel and isolate processes (light, fast). VMs run a full guest OS on a hypervisor (heavier, stronger isolation).

**Q. Why use multi-stage Docker builds?**
A. To build with heavy tools in one stage and copy only the artefact into a small runtime image: smaller, faster and more secure.

**Q. How do containers keep data?**
A. Through volumes (or bind mounts). The container filesystem is ephemeral.

**Q. Pod vs Deployment vs Service?**
A. A pod runs containers. A Deployment manages replicated pods and rolling updates. A Service gives the pods a stable name/IP and load balances across them.

**Q. Liveness vs readiness probe?**
A. Readiness decides whether the pod receives traffic. Liveness decides whether the container should be restarted.

**Q. ConfigMap vs Secret?**
A. A ConfigMap holds non-sensitive config. A Secret holds sensitive data (base64-encoded, and it should be encrypted at rest and access-controlled).

**Q. How does Kubernetes do zero-downtime deployments?**
A. Rolling updates with readiness probes: new pods must be ready before old ones are removed (maxUnavailable 0).

**Q. What is CI/CD?**
A. CI automatically builds and tests every change. CD automatically packages and deploys passing builds to environments, often with approval gates for production.

**Q. How do you roll back a bad deployment?**
A. `kubectl rollout undo`, or redeploy the previous image tag (images tagged by commit SHA). Blue-green deployments allow an instant switch back.

**Q. How do you handle secrets in CI/CD?**
A. Store them in the CI secret store / a vault, inject them at runtime as environment variables, never commit them, and rotate them regularly.

name: Phase 11 — Cloud (Optional)
description: Cloud models and the AWS/GCP/Azure services that map to this stack
content:
# Phase 11: Cloud (optional)

The TOR lists cloud as **optional**. Knowing the basic ideas and which managed service replaces which part of your stack is enough.

name: Cloud Fundamentals and Service Mapping
description: IaaS/PaaS/SaaS, regions, managed services, shared responsibility
content:
# Cloud fundamentals

## Service models

| Model | You manage | Provider manages | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **IaaS** | OS, runtime, app, data | Hardware, network, virtualization | AWS EC2, Azure VM |
| **PaaS** | App + data | Everything below | AWS Elastic Beanstalk, Azure App Service, Cloud Run |
| **SaaS** | Just use it | Everything | Gmail, Office 365 |

**Analogy (pizza):** IaaS = they give you the kitchen and you cook. PaaS = they give you the dough and oven, and you add toppings. SaaS = pizza delivered to your door.

## Key ideas
- **Region / Availability Zone (AZ):** a region is a geographic area. AZs are separate data centres within it. Deploy across **2+ AZs** for high availability.
- **Elasticity:** scale up or down automatically with load, and pay for what you use.
- **Shared responsibility:** the provider secures the cloud (hardware, data centres). **You** secure what you put **in** the cloud (IAM, data, network rules, patches on your VMs).
- **IAM:** users, roles and policies. Follow **least privilege**, and give apps roles instead of hard-coded keys.

## Mapping our stack to managed services

| Our component | AWS | GCP | Azure |
|---|---|---|---|
| VM | EC2 | Compute Engine | Virtual Machines |
| Kubernetes | EKS | GKE | AKS |
| Run containers simply | ECS/Fargate, App Runner | Cloud Run | Container Apps |
| PostgreSQL | RDS / Aurora | Cloud SQL | Azure Database for PostgreSQL |
| Redis | ElastiCache | Memorystore | Azure Cache for Redis |
| File storage | S3 | Cloud Storage | Blob Storage |
| Container registry | ECR | Artifact Registry | ACR |
| Secrets | Secrets Manager | Secret Manager | Key Vault |
| Messaging | SQS/SNS, MSK (Kafka) | Pub/Sub | Service Bus, Event Hubs |
| Monitoring | CloudWatch | Cloud Monitoring | Azure Monitor |
| CDN | CloudFront | Cloud CDN | Front Door |

## Example: a production-style AWS layout
```
Users → CloudFront (React static files from S3)
      → ALB (HTTPS) → EKS pods (loan-api, in private subnets across 2 AZs)
                          ├── RDS PostgreSQL (Multi-AZ, automated backups)
                          ├── ElastiCache Redis
                          └── Secrets Manager (DB password)
CloudWatch for logs/metrics; IAM roles for pods (IRSA)
```
**Why each piece**
- S3 + CloudFront: cheap, fast global delivery of static frontend files.
- ALB: a managed load balancer that terminates HTTPS.
- **Private subnets:** the app and DB are not directly reachable from the internet.
- RDS **Multi-AZ:** a standby copy in another AZ with automatic failover, plus backups and point-in-time restore without you running pg_dump.
- Secrets Manager + IAM roles: no passwords in code or config files.

**Infrastructure as Code (IaC):** define the cloud resources in code (**Terraform**, CloudFormation) so that environments are reproducible and reviewed like application code.

**Data residency note for PKSF:** financial and personal data may need to stay in Bangladesh (a local data centre / government cloud). Mention that you would check the regulations before choosing a region.

name: Phase 12 — System Design
description: Scalability concepts, approach and a full PO loan system case study
content:
# Phase 12: System design

The viva may ask you to "design a loan management system for 200+ POs". They're testing **structured thinking**, not a perfect answer.

name: System Design Fundamentals
description: Scaling, load balancing, caching, replication, sharding, CAP, queues
content:
# System design fundamentals

## Scaling
- **Vertical (scale up):** a bigger machine (more CPU/RAM). Simple, but it has a ceiling and is a single point of failure.
- **Horizontal (scale out):** more machines behind a load balancer. Needs **stateless** apps (sessions in Redis/JWT, files in object storage).
- **Analogy:** vertical = hiring one super-fast cashier. Horizontal = opening more cash counters.

## Building blocks

| Block | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Load balancer** | Spreads traffic, removes unhealthy instances (round-robin, least connections) |
| **Cache** (Redis, CDN) | Serves hot data fast and reduces DB load |
| **Read replicas** | Serve reports/reads, and the primary handles writes |
| **Sharding / partitioning** | Split data across DBs/partitions (e.g. by PO or by year) |
| **Message queue** | Absorb spikes, async work, decouple services |
| **Object storage** | Files (documents, photos) instead of DB blobs |
| **CDN** | Static assets close to users |

## Key concepts
- **Latency vs throughput:** the time for one request vs the requests per second.
- **Availability:** 99.9% ≈ 8.7 hours of downtime per year. 99.99% ≈ 52 minutes. Achieve it through redundancy (no single point of failure), health checks and failover.
- **CAP:** during a network partition, choose consistency or availability. **Money data → choose consistency.** A dashboard counter → availability is fine.
- **Consistency models:** strong (read your latest write) vs eventual (replicas catch up within seconds).
- **Idempotency:** retried requests must not double-charge.
- **Back-of-the-envelope estimation:**
  200 POs × 500 officers = 100,000 users. 5 million members, 1 repayment per week each ≈ 5M / (6 working days × 8 h × 3600 s) ≈ **30 writes/s on average**, maybe **10× at peak (≈300/s)** on collection days. That is very manageable for one well-tuned PostgreSQL primary. **Don't over-engineer.**

**Analogy:** system design is like planning a city's roads. First estimate the traffic, then decide how many lanes, which bypasses and where to put traffic lights. You don't build a 12-lane highway to a village.

name: Approach to Any Design Question
description: A step-by-step framework to answer in a viva
content:
# How to answer any design question

**Follow these steps out loud.** Interviewers grade the process.

1. **Clarify requirements (2–3 min)**
   - Functional: what must it do? (register members, disburse loans, collect repayments, PAR reports)
   - Non-functional: how many users? Peak load? Availability? Security/compliance? Offline field use?
2. **Estimate scale:** users, requests per second, data size per year. Decide whether "one DB is enough".
3. **High-level design:** draw the boxes: clients → gateway → services → DB/cache/queue.
4. **Data model:** the main tables/entities and their relationships, plus the key indexes.
5. **API design:** 4–6 key endpoints.
6. **Deep dive** into 1–2 hard parts: consistency of payments, reports at scale, security.
7. **Bottlenecks and trade-offs:** what fails first, and how you would scale it. Admit the trade-offs ("I chose X over Y because...").
8. **Operations:** monitoring, backups, deployment, audit.

**Phrases that score well**
- "Let me first clarify the requirements…"
- "For money, I'd prioritise consistency over availability, so a single PostgreSQL primary with ACID transactions."
- "This is read-heavy, so I'd add a cache / read replica / materialized view for reports."
- "To avoid double posting I'd use an idempotency key with a unique constraint."
- "I'd start as a modular monolith and extract services when needed."

**Analogy:** like a doctor's consultation: ask about the symptoms (requirements), examine (estimate), diagnose (design), prescribe (trade-offs), follow up (monitoring).

name: Case Study: PO Loan Management System
description: End-to-end design for PKSF-style microfinance
content:
# Case study: PO loan management system

## 1. Requirements
- **Functional:** manage POs, branches, samities, members; loan products; loan application → approval → disbursement; installment schedules; record repayments (including from field officers' phones); savings; overdue tracking; PAR and portfolio reports for PKSF; audit history.
- **Non-functional:** 100k users; correctness of money (no lost or double payments); role- and PO-based data isolation; 99.9% availability; reports over millions of rows; partly **offline** field collection; full audit trail.

## 2. High-level architecture
```
 Field app (React PWA / mobile)   PO web (React)    PKSF HQ dashboards
            \                         |                  /
             └──────── HTTPS ── API Gateway / Nginx ────┘
                              │   (JWT from Keycloak)
          ┌───────────────────┼──────────────────────────┐
          ▼                   ▼                          ▼
   member module        loan module               collection module
   (members, KYC)   (products, schedule,      (repayments, ledger,
                     approval workflow)          receipts, idempotency)
          └──────────── PostgreSQL primary (ACID) ─────────┘
                              │ streaming replication
                              ▼
                     read replica → reporting module (PAR, MIS, materialized views)
  Redis: cache (POs, products), rate limits      Kafka/outbox: events → SMS, analytics
  Object storage: KYC documents                  Prometheus/Grafana, ELK, backups (PITR)
```
- Start as a **modular monolith** (one deployable, modules with clear boundaries). Extract reporting or notification services later if needed.

## 3. Data model (core)
```sql
po(id, code, name)
branch(id, po_id, name)
samity(id, branch_id, name, meeting_day)
member(id, samity_id, national_id UNIQUE, name, phone, status)
loan_product(id, name, rate, method, max_months)
loan(id, member_id, product_id, principal, outstanding, status, disbursed_on, version)
installment(id, loan_id, seq_no, due_date, amount, paid_amount, UNIQUE(loan_id, seq_no))
ledger_entry(id, loan_id, type, amount, reference UNIQUE, reverses_id, posted_at, posted_by)
audit_log(id, entity, entity_id, action, old_value JSONB, new_value JSONB, user_id, at)
```
- **Indexes:** `member(samity_id)`, `loan(member_id, status)`, partial `installment(due_date) WHERE paid_amount < amount`, `ledger_entry(loan_id, posted_at)`.
- **Multi-tenancy:** every query is scoped by the user's `po_id` (taken from the JWT claim). Optionally use PostgreSQL **Row-Level Security** as a second safety net.

## 4. Key APIs
```http
POST /api/v1/loans                         # apply
POST /api/v1/loans/{id}/approve            # MANAGER only
POST /api/v1/loans/{id}/disburse
POST /api/v1/repayments                    # header: Idempotency-Key
GET  /api/v1/loans/{id}/schedule
GET  /api/v1/reports/par?poId=7&asOf=2025-11-30
```

## 5. Deep dive: recording a repayment safely
```java
@Transactional
public Receipt repay(String idemKey, RepaymentRequest r) {
    Loan loan = loans.findByIdForUpdate(r.loanId()).orElseThrow();      // 1. row lock
    checkPoAccess(loan);                                                 // 2. authorization
    if (r.amount().compareTo(loan.getOutstanding()) > 0) throw new BusinessRuleException("Overpayment");
    ledger.save(LedgerEntry.repayment(loan, r.amount(), idemKey));       // 3. UNIQUE(reference) blocks duplicates
    allocateToInstallments(loan, r.amount());                            // 4. oldest due first
    loan.reduceOutstanding(r.amount());
    outbox.save(new OutboxEvent("RepaymentRecorded", loan.getId()));     // 5. SMS receipt, async
    return Receipt.of(loan, r);
}
```
**Why each step**
1. `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`: two officers paying the same loan at the same moment can't lose an update.
2. An officer can only touch loans in their own PO (prevents broken access control).
3. A retry with the same idempotency key hits the unique constraint, so the original receipt is returned instead of double-posting.
4. The payment clears the oldest installments first (standard microfinance practice).
5. The outbox guarantees the SMS event is published if, and only if, the payment committed.
- Everything happens in **one ACID transaction**: either all of it or none.

## 6. Offline field collection
- The PWA stores repayments locally (IndexedDB) with a client-generated **UUID idempotency key**, and syncs when back online. Duplicate syncs are harmless because of step 3.

## 7. Reports at scale
- Heavy PAR/portfolio queries run on a **read replica** or **materialized views** refreshed nightly, plus a Redis cache for dashboards. They never slow down the collection workload on the primary.
- Partition `ledger_entry` by year as the data grows.

## 8. Security and operations
- Keycloak (SSO, MFA for managers), roles plus PO scoping, TLS everywhere, encrypted NIDs, immutable ledger, Envers audit.
- Kubernetes with 3+ replicas across zones, HPA, readiness probes, rolling deploys.
- Monitoring: request latency, error rate, DB connections, failed logins. Daily backups plus WAL archiving (PITR), with restores tested.

**Trade-offs to mention:** a monolith first (simpler, ACID) instead of microservices; pessimistic locking on the loan row (correctness over raw throughput, which is fine at about 300 writes/s); eventual consistency for reports (minutes old is acceptable).

name: Phase 12 — Interview Questions
description: Quick Q&A revision for system design
content:
# Phase 12 interview questions

**Q. Vertical vs horizontal scaling?**
A. Vertical means a bigger machine (simple, limited, single point of failure). Horizontal means more machines behind a load balancer (needs stateless services, scales further).

**Q. How do you make a service stateless?**
A. Keep no user session in memory: use JWT or Redis-backed sessions, store files in object storage, and keep all state in the DB/cache.

**Q. How would you design for high availability?**
A. Redundancy at every layer (multiple app instances across zones, DB with a standby/failover), health checks, load balancers, backups, and no single point of failure.

**Q. When do you add a cache?**
A. For read-heavy data that tolerates slight staleness, when the DB is a bottleneck. Plan invalidation and TTLs.

**Q. How do you scale reads vs writes in PostgreSQL?**
A. Reads: replicas, caching, materialized views. Writes: tune queries and indexes, batch, partition, and as a last resort shard by tenant (PO).

**Q. How do you ensure a payment is not processed twice?**
A. An idempotency key with a unique constraint, done in a transaction with row locking, and idempotent consumers for events.

**Q. How do you keep one PO from seeing another PO's data?**
A. A PO id claim in the token, every query filtered by it in the service layer, method-level security checks, and optionally PostgreSQL row-level security.

**Q. What would you monitor in production?**
A. Latency (p95/p99), error rate, throughput, saturation (CPU, memory, DB pool, disk), business metrics (repayments per hour), and security events (failed logins).

# Project scope: PO microfinance management system

## Features (MVP first, then extras)
**MVP**

2. CRUD for POs, samities and members (validation, pagination, search).
3. Loan products and loan applications → approval (MANAGER) → disbursement.
4. Installment schedule generation (flat/declining interest via the Strategy pattern).
5. Record repayments with an idempotency key, a ledger, and optimistic/pessimistic locking.
6. Dashboard: total outstanding, overdue, PAR per PO.

**Extras**
- Redis cache for products/POs, a rate limit on login.
- A nightly overdue job with ShedLock.
- Kafka/outbox → notification service (SMS mock).
- A SOAP endpoint for a "bank balance check" integration.
- Audit history with Envers.
- Kubernetes manifests + GitHub Actions CI/CD.

## Tech stack
Java 21 · Spring Boot 3 · Spring Security (resource server) · Spring Data JPA · Flyway · PostgreSQL 16 · Redis · Keycloak · React 18 + TypeScript + Vite · TanStack Query · React Hook Form + Zod · JUnit 5 · Mockito · Testcontainers · Vitest + RTL · Docker · docker-compose · GitHub Actions · (Kubernetes)

## Repository layout
```
po-microfinance/
├── backend/
│   ├── src/main/java/bd/org/pksf/mf/
│   │   ├── common/        (config, security, exceptions, audit)
│   │   ├── member/        (controller, service, repository, entity, dto)
│   │   ├── loan/
│   │   ├── collection/
│   │   └── report/
│   ├── src/main/resources/db/migration/   (Flyway V1__...sql)
│   ├── src/test/java/...                  (unit + Testcontainers tests)
│   └── Dockerfile
├── frontend/
│   ├── src/{api,components,pages,hooks,types}
│   └── Dockerfile

├── k8s/                     (deployment, service, ingress, hpa)
├── docker-compose.yml
├── .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

- `realm-pksf.json`: a reviewer gets working users and roles with zero manual setup.
- `docker-compose.yml` at the root: **one command runs everything**.

name: Written Test Strategy
description: Time management, MCQ tactics, writing code by hand
content:
# Written test strategy

## Before the exam
- Do **timed** MCQ sets (e.g. 50 questions in 40 minutes).
- Write 2–3 programs **on paper** every day: string reversal, palindrome, duplicates, binary search, sorting, linked list reverse, second largest, an SQL query with a JOIN + GROUP BY.
- Revise the "Interview Questions" topic of every phase in this guide.

## During the exam
1. **Read every question to the end.** Watch for "NOT", "EXCEPT", "always".
2. **Easy questions first.** Mark the hard ones and come back.
3. MCQs: eliminate the clearly wrong options, then choose. Don't leave blanks unless there's negative marking.
4. **Handwritten code:**
   - Write the method signature first, then handle the **edge cases** (null, empty, a single element).
   - Use clear variable names and consistent indentation.
   - Add one line of comment for the idea ("two pointers from both ends").
   - Dry-run with a small example in the margin.
   - State the time/space complexity at the end; it earns extra credit.
5. **SQL:** write the FROM/JOIN first, then WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY. Check that every non-aggregated column is in GROUP BY.
6. **Theory answers:** definition → short example → one advantage/disadvantage. Short and structured beats long and vague.

## Example of a strong handwritten answer
```java
// Returns the first non-repeating character, or '_' if none. O(n) time, O(1) space (26 letters).
char firstUnique(String s) {
    if (s == null || s.isEmpty()) return '_';
    int[] count = new int[26];
    for (char c : s.toCharArray()) count[c - 'a']++;     // pass 1: count
    for (char c : s.toCharArray())
        if (count[c - 'a'] == 1) return c;               // pass 2: first with count 1
    return '_';
}
```
**Why it scores well**
- An edge-case check first (null/empty).
- A comment states the purpose and the complexity.
- Two simple passes, easy for the examiner to follow.
- `c - 'a'` maps a letter to an index 0–25 (assuming lowercase a–z, which you should say explicitly).

# Viva preparation

## 1. Your project walkthrough (practise until smooth)
A 2-minute script:
1. **Problem:** "POs need to track loans and repayments accurately…"
2. **Architecture:** draw the boxes: React → Spring Boot → PostgreSQL/Redis, Keycloak.
3. **One hard problem you solved:** "Preventing double repayments: I used an idempotency key with a unique constraint plus row locking…"
4. **Testing and deployment:** "Unit tests with Mockito, integration tests with Testcontainers, CI on GitHub Actions, docker-compose."
5. **What you'd improve:** shows maturity ("I'd add a read replica for reports").

## 2. STAR format for experience questions
**S**ituation → **T**ask → **A**ction → **R**esult (with numbers if possible).

> "Tell me about a performance problem you fixed."
> **S:** The loan list page took 8 seconds. **T:** I had to make it fast without changing the UI. **A:** SQL logs showed an N+1 problem: 1 + 200 queries. I replaced it with a DTO projection using a join, and added an index on `loan(member_id, status)`. **R:** The page loaded in 300 ms and DB CPU dropped by 40%.

## 3. Likely questions and how to answer

**"Why PKSF?"**
Link your skills to their mission: "PKSF's systems support financial inclusion for millions through 200+ POs. I want to build secure, reliable systems where correctness really matters, and my Spring Boot/React/PostgreSQL experience fits directly."

**"Tell me about yourself."** (60–90 seconds)
Present (current role and stack) → past (key projects/achievements) → future (why this job).

**"What is your biggest weakness?"**
A real but non-critical weakness plus what you're doing about it: "I used to over-engineer early; now I start simple and refactor when the need is proven."

**"How do you keep learning?"** Official docs, building side projects (like your portfolio), reading engineering blogs.

**"A loan balance is wrong in production. What do you do?"**
1. Stop further damage (if needed, block that operation).
2. Check the **audit logs and ledger** to see exactly what happened.
3. Reproduce it in a test environment and write a failing test.
4. Fix the bug, and correct the data with **reversal/adjustment entries** (never silent edits), with approval.
5. Root-cause analysis plus prevention (a constraint, a test, monitoring).

**"How do you handle disagreement with a colleague?"**
Listen, discuss with data/prototypes, agree on criteria, escalate respectfully if needed, and commit to the team decision.

## 4. Technical "explain this" checklist (practise out loud, 1 minute each)
- How a request flows: browser → Nginx → Spring Security filter → controller → service → repository → DB.
- How JWT/Keycloak login works.
- @Transactional and why it sometimes fails.
- The N+1 problem and its fixes.
- Optimistic vs pessimistic locking.
- How an index works and when it isn't used.
- Docker vs VM; Kubernetes liveness vs readiness.
- useEffect and its dependency array.

**Tip:** if you don't know something, say "I haven't used that directly, but here's how I'd approach it…" Honesty plus reasoning beats bluffing.

description: One-line answers to revise the night before
content:
# Rapid-fire revision list

Cover the right side and test yourself.

## CS and Java
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Binary search complexity | O(log n), sorted input |
| Stable O(n log n) sort | Merge sort / TimSort |
| HashMap default capacity / load factor | 16 / 0.75 |
| Bucket becomes a tree at | > 8 entries (capacity ≥ 64) |
| String immutable why | Security, thread safety, hash caching, pool |
| `==` vs `equals` | Reference vs content |
| equals/hashCode contract | Equal objects → equal hash codes |
| Checked exception example | IOException |
| `volatile` gives | Visibility, not atomicity |
| `start()` vs `run()` | New thread vs same thread |
| Heap vs stack | Objects (shared) vs frames (per thread) |
| Default GC (Java 9+) | G1 |
| Money type | BigDecimal + NUMERIC |
| SOLID | SRP, OCP, LSP, ISP, DIP |
| Deadlock conditions | Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait |
| TCP handshake | SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK |
| 401 vs 403 | Not authenticated vs not authorized |
| Idempotent methods | GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS |

## Spring
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| @SpringBootApplication = | @SpringBootConfiguration + @EnableAutoConfiguration + @ComponentScan |
| Default bean scope | Singleton |
| Preferred injection | Constructor |
| Default propagation | REQUIRED |
| Rollback by default on | Unchecked exceptions |
| @Transactional fails when | Self-invocation, private method, checked/swallowed exception |
| N+1 fix | JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, DTO projection, batch size |
| Optimistic lock | @Version → 409 on conflict |
| Pessimistic lock | SELECT ... FOR UPDATE |
| @ManyToOne default fetch | EAGER (set LAZY) |
| ddl-auto in prod | validate / none + Flyway |
| Validation trigger | @Valid on @RequestBody |
| Global errors | @RestControllerAdvice + ProblemDetail |

## Database
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| WHERE vs HAVING | Rows before grouping vs groups after |
| SQL logical order | FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT |
| RANK vs DENSE_RANK (100,100,90) | 1,1,3 vs 1,1,2 |
| Postgres default isolation | Read Committed |
| 3NF | Non-key columns depend only on the key |
| Composite index rule | Leftmost prefix |
| Index ignored when | Function on column, leading %, type cast, low selectivity |
| Read a plan | EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) |
| MVCC cleanup | VACUUM (autovacuum) |
| Deep pagination fix | Keyset (WHERE id > last) |

## Security, Redis, microservices
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Password storage | BCrypt / Argon2 (salted, slow hash) |
| JWT parts | Header . Payload . Signature (payload not encrypted) |
| SPA login flow | Authorization Code + PKCE |
| Service-to-service flow | Client Credentials |
| OIDC adds | ID token (authentication) |
| Keycloak roles claim | realm_access.roles → map to ROLE_ |
| CSRF can be disabled for | Stateless APIs that use Authorization headers |
| Most common cache pattern | Cache-aside |
| Cache invalidation on write | Evict (delete), plus a TTL |
| Distributed lock | SET key val NX PX ttl / Redisson / ShedLock |
| Circuit breaker states | Closed → Open → Half-open |
| Cross-service transaction | Saga + outbox |
| Kafka ordering | Within a partition (same key) |

## Frontend and DevOps
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Event loop order | Sync → microtasks (promises) → macrotasks (timers) |
| `[]` deps in useEffect | Run once after mount |
| useMemo vs useCallback | Value vs function |
| List keys | Stable unique IDs, not indexes |
| Server state lib | TanStack Query |
| Image vs container | Template vs running instance |
| Multi-stage build | Small, secure runtime image |
| Readiness vs liveness | Receive traffic? vs restart? |
| Zero-downtime deploy | Rolling update + readiness probe |
| Safe undo on a shared branch | git revert |

**Last night before the exam:** revise this list once, sleep well, and arrive early. Good luck!
